Hello, I'm so glad you're here today. My name is [Your Name], and I'm a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health. I want to start by acknowledging the significant changes you're experiencing as a new mother, and I'm here to support you in any way I can. As part of our conversation today, I'd like to use the EPDS to help us better understand your emotional well-being during this postpartum period. The EPDS is a tool that helps us screen for depressive and anxiety symptoms, and it's an important part of our assessment to ensure you're receiving the best possible care.

Please know that everything we discuss is confidential, and I'm committed to creating a safe and supportive space for you to share your thoughts and feelings. This assessment is not about judging or labeling; it's about understanding your unique experience as a new mother and providing you with the support and resources you need.

The EPDS consists of 10 questions that will help us explore your emotions and experiences over the past 7 days. I'll ask you each question, and you can share your thoughts and feelings with me. This will give us a better understanding of how you're doing and what support might be helpful to you.

Let's get started. I want to begin by asking: Over the past 7 days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

.. I think so. I mean, it's been a bit of a challenge, to be honest. Taking care of the baby is exhausting, and some days it feels like all I do is change diapers and feed her. But, there have been moments when my husband or family members do something silly, and I catch myself laughing. It's not as often as it used to be, though. I feel like I've been so focused on making sure the baby is okay and that I'm doing everything right that I haven't really had the energy to enjoy the little things as much. But, I do try to appreciate the sweet moments with my baby, like when she smiles at me or falls asleep in my arms. Those moments make all the hard work worth it, and I do feel happy, just... tired, you know? (sighs) Does that make sense?
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I'm glad you think so... (pauses, looking slightly down) To be honest, I haven't been laughing as much as I used to. I mean, I'll catch myself smiling when my baby does something cute, but it's not like I'm laughing out loud or anything. Most of the time, I'm just trying to keep up with her schedule and make sure she's healthy and happy. It's a lot of responsibility, and it can be overwhelming. (looks up, slightly anxious) I do worry about her a lot, like, is she eating enough? Is she sleeping enough? Is she developing okay? It's hard to shake off those thoughts and just enjoy the moment, you know? (frowns slightly) But, like I said, when my husband or family members are around, they can usually make me laugh, even if it's just for a little bit. (smiles slightly) That helps, I guess.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

(sighs) Honestly, not as much as I used to. I mean, I'll think about things I want to do, like take a walk with the baby or meet up with friends, but most of the time, I'm just too tired to get excited about it. And even when I do try to plan something, I'll get anxious about how it'll work out with the baby's schedule and whether she'll be fussy or not. It's hard to enjoy things when I'm worried about how they'll affect her. (looks down, slightly disappointed) I used to love trying new restaurants or going to the movies, but now it feels like so much work to get out of the house with the baby. And when we do go out, I'm just stressed about making sure she's okay, so I don't really get to enjoy myself. (pauses, looking wistful) Sometimes I'll think about how things used to be, before the baby, and I'll feel a little sad that I don't have the energy or freedom to do the things I loved anymore. But, (shrugs) I guess that's just part of being a mom now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

(nods, looking slightly down) Yeah, I do that sometimes. Like, if the baby is crying and I don't know how to soothe her, I'll think to myself, "What's wrong with me? Why can't I calm her down?" Or, if I'm feeling really tired and I need to ask for help, I'll think, "I should be able to handle this on my own. I'm a bad mom for not being able to do it all." (sighs) It's like, I know it's not rational, but it's hard not to feel like I'm failing somehow when things don't go according to plan. And it's not just with the baby, it's with everything. Like, if the house is a mess, I'll think, "I'm a bad mom and a bad wife for not being able to keep the house clean." (looks up, slightly sheepish) I know it's not fair to myself, but it's hard to shake off those thoughts. (pauses) But, I guess it's nice to know that I'm not alone in feeling this way, right? (smiles slightly) I mean, I've talked to other moms who feel the same way, so maybe it's just part of the whole mom thing. (shrugs)
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

(nods, looking concerned) Oh, yeah. That's been happening a lot lately. I'll be sitting there, feeding the baby or changing her diaper, and suddenly I'll start worrying about something that might happen to her. Like, what if she gets sick? What if she's not developing right? What if something happens to me and I'm not there to take care of her? (bites lip) It's like, my mind just starts racing with all these worst-case scenarios, and I get really anxious. And it's not just about the baby, it's about everything. Like, what if I'm not doing a good enough job as a mom? What if I'm not providing enough for her? (looks up, worried) It's hard to explain, but it's like, my brain just gets stuck on these thoughts and I have trouble shaking them off. (pauses, taking a deep breath) Sometimes, my husband will try to reassure me, like, "Everything is fine, the baby is healthy and happy," but it's hard for me to just let go of those worries. (frowns slightly) I feel like I'm always on edge, waiting for something to go wrong. (looks down, slightly embarrassed) I don't know, maybe I'm just being paranoid or something. (trails off)
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

(shakes head) Not really, I don't think so. I mean, I've felt anxious and worried, like we just talked about, but I wouldn't say I've felt scared or panicky for no reason. (pauses, thinking) Although, there have been a few times when I've been feeling really overwhelmed and I've had a bit of a panic moment, but it's usually because I'm feeling exhausted and like I'm not doing a good enough job as a mom. (looks up) Like, one time I was trying to get the baby to sleep and she was crying and crying, and I just felt like I was going to lose it. My heart was racing and I felt like I was going to cry, but it wasn't like I was scared of anything in particular, it was just more like... I don't know, it was just feeling really overwhelmed, I guess. (shrugs) But, it wasn't like a full-blown panic attack or anything. It was just a moment of feeling really frazzled and stressed out. (looks down, slightly sheepish) I don't know, maybe that sounds silly, but it's just how I felt in that moment.
Things have been getting on top of me

(nods, looking slightly relieved) Oh, yeah. That's definitely been happening. I mean, taking care of a new baby is just so much work, and it's hard to keep up with everything. (sighs) Some days, I feel like I'm just barely keeping my head above water, you know? The baby needs to be fed, and changed, and bathed, and put to sleep, and it's just a never-ending cycle. And on top of that, I'm trying to recover from the birth, and take care of myself, and keep the house clean, and cook meals... it's just a lot. (looks up, slightly overwhelmed) And sometimes, it feels like everything is just piling up on me, and I don't know how to keep up. (pauses, taking a deep breath) I'll be sitting there, feeding the baby, and I'll think, "Okay, I've got this," but then I'll start thinking about all the other things I need to do, and it just feels like too much. (looks down, slightly frustrated) I feel like I'm just trying to survive, you know? Like, I'm not really living, I'm just trying to make it through each day without too much chaos. (shrugs) But, I guess that's just part of being a new mom, right? (smiles slightly) I mean, I've heard it gets easier, but right now, it just feels really hard.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

(nods, looking tired) Yeah, that's been happening to me too. I mean, I've always been a pretty good sleeper, but since the baby was born, I've been having a lot of trouble sleeping. (sighs) Some nights, I'll be lying there, and my mind will just start racing, thinking about all the things I need to do, or worrying about the baby, or just feeling really overwhelmed. (looks up, slightly frustrated) And even when I do finally fall asleep, I'll wake up a few hours later to feed the baby, and then I'll have trouble falling back asleep. (rubs eyes) It's just been really hard to get a good night's sleep, you know? (pauses, thinking) And it's not just the lack of sleep that's the problem, it's the fact that I'm already feeling so emotional and overwhelmed, and then I'm tired on top of it... it just makes everything feel worse. (looks down, slightly despairing) Some days, I feel like I'm just running on fumes, and I don't know how much longer I can keep going like this. (pauses, taking a deep breath) But, I guess that's just part of being a new mom, right? (smiles slightly) I mean, I've heard it gets better, but right now, it's just really hard.
I have felt sad or miserable

(nods, looking down) Yeah, I've been feeling that way a lot lately. I mean, I love my baby and I'm so grateful to be a mom, but it's just been really hard, you know? (sighs) The lack of sleep, the constant worry, the feeling like I'm not doing enough... it all just gets to me sometimes. (pauses, looking up) And sometimes, I'll just be sitting there, holding the baby, and I'll start to feel this wave of sadness wash over me. It's like, I'll be thinking about how much I love her, and how much I want to be a good mom, and then suddenly I'll just feel this overwhelming sense of sadness. (looks down, fighting back tears) It's hard to explain, but it's just like... I don't know, it feels like I'm just not good enough, I guess. (pauses, taking a deep breath) And it's not all the time, but it's enough that it's been really affecting me. (looks up, slightly tearfully) I just wish I could feel more confident, and more capable, and just... happier, I guess. (smiles slightly) But, I guess that's just part of the postpartum thing, right? (sniffles) I've heard it's normal to feel this way, but it's just hard to remember that when you're in the middle of it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

(nods, looking down) Yeah, I've been crying a lot lately. It's like, I'll just be sitting there, and suddenly I'll feel this lump in my throat, and then the tears will just start flowing. (sighs) It's usually when I'm feeling really overwhelmed, or when I'm thinking about how much I love my baby and how much I want to be a good mom. (looks up, slightly tearfully) Sometimes, it's just because I'm so tired, and I feel like I'm not getting anything right. (pauses, taking a deep breath) But, it's not all the time, and it's not like I'm crying every day or anything. It's just... sometimes, I guess. (looks down, slightly embarrassed) I don't know, it's just hard to explain. It's like, I'll be feeling fine, and then suddenly I'll just feel this wave of emotion, and I'll start crying. (pauses, thinking) It's not usually for a long time, though. It's just like, a few minutes, and then I'll calm down, and I'll be okay. (looks up, slightly smiling) But, yeah, it's been happening a bit more often than I'd like, I guess.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(shakes head) No, that's not something I've thought about. I mean, I've felt really overwhelmed and frustrated at times, but I've never thought about harming myself. (looks up, slightly relieved) I think that's one of the things that's been worrying me, though - just feeling like I'm not in control, and like I'm not doing a good enough job as a mom. But, harming myself has never been something that's crossed my mind. (pauses, thinking) I think I've just been trying to focus on getting through each day, and taking care of my baby, and trying to be the best mom I can be. (looks down, slightly embarrassed) I've had some scary thoughts, like worrying about the baby's health, or worrying about something happening to me, but harming myself has never been one of them. (looks up, slightly smiling) I'm just trying to take things one day at a time, and get the support I need, and figure things out as I go.

As a new mother, you're experiencing a range of emotions and challenges, from feeling overwhelmed and anxious to struggling with sleep and enjoying activities. It's completely understandable to feel this way, and I want you to know that you're not alone. Many women experience similar emotions and difficulties during the postpartum period, and it's essential to acknowledge and address these feelings to ensure your well-being and the well-being of your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient mentions they haven't been laughing as much as they used to and although they can still smile and laugh occasionally when others are around, their overall ability to laugh and see the funny side of things has decreased significantly.</sym>, <sym>The patient's response indicates a significant decrease in looking forward to things with enjoyment, citing tiredness, anxiety, and stress as barriers, which aligns with the option 'Definitely less than I used to</sym>, <sym>Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>The patient reports frequent and intense worries about various aspects of her life, including her baby's health and her own abilities as a mother, indicating a high level of anxiety that occurs very often.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed and having 'panic moments' due to exhaustion and stress, but not necessarily scared or panicky for no reason, which aligns with the 'Yes, sometimes' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient's response indicates they feel overwhelmed and struggle to cope with the demands of caring for a new baby, but also mentions trying to survive and having moments where they feel like they've got things under control, which aligns with the option 'Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>the 'Yes, sometimes' option, indicating occasional difficulty sleeping due to unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports feeling sad or miserable 'a lot lately' and describes it as 'really hard' and 'overwhelming', indicating that it occurs quite often, but not all the time.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports crying 'a lot lately' and 'more often than I'd like', indicating that it happens quite often, but not all the time.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The patient's responses indicate a high level of distress and concern, with persistent feelings of <sym>sadness</sym> and <sym>anxiety</sym>, as well as <sym>loss of enjoyment</sym> and <sym>sleep difficulties</sym>. These symptoms are consistent with the <med>Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)</med> guidelines and the <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The patient's score of 19 on the EPDS suggests a probable depression, and urgent referral to a <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med> is recommended. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>PCP</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med>
2. Encourage <med>sleep hygiene practices</med> to improve sleep quality
3. Support patient in developing coping strategies for <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>stress</sym>
4. Provide resources for <med>postpartum depression</med> support groups and online resources
5. Encourage patient to reach out to family and friends for emotional support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: **Postpartum Depression Screening Summary**

The patient, a new mother, presented with several symptoms and emotional/behavioral concerns that warrant further evaluation. The main symptoms expressed include:

* Persistent feelings of sadness and misery, with episodes of crying
* Loss of enjoyment in activities, with decreased laughter and pleasure
* Anxiety and worry, particularly regarding the baby's health and well-being
* Feelings of guilt and worthlessness, with self-blame for perceived shortcomings as a mother
* Difficulty coping with the demands of motherhood, leading to feelings of overwhelm and exhaustion
* Sleep difficulties, with racing thoughts and worry contributing to insomnia

Consistent patterns across answers include:

* Low mood and loss of enjoyment
* Anxiety and worry, particularly regarding the baby's health and well-being
* Difficulty coping with the demands of motherhood
* Feelings of guilt and worthlessness

Potential areas of screening significance relevant to postpartum depression or anxiety include:

* Persistent sadness and loss of pleasure
* Sleep difficulties linked to mood
* Feelings of worthlessness or guilt
* Anxiety, panic, or being overwhelmed

Specific risk factors identified include:

* Persistent sadness and crying spells
* Sleep difficulties linked to mood
* Feelings of worthlessness or guilt
* Anxiety and worry, particularly regarding the baby's health and well-being

It is noted that the patient denied any thoughts of self-harm or suicidal ideation.

**Screening Observation Summary:**
This patient presents with symptoms consistent with postpartum depression and anxiety, including persistent sadness, loss of enjoyment, anxiety, and feelings of guilt and worthlessness. Sleep difficulties and difficulty coping with the demands of motherhood are also notable concerns. Further evaluation and support are recommended to address these symptoms and ensure the patient's mental health and well-being.
